body: THE GOOD NUMBER: Cox & Kings had a famous brand, reported profits and an international footprint, and looked like a cheap way to own Indian outbound travel. WHY IT LIED: travel operators collect money from customers before paying hotels and airlines, so the model should run on negative working capital and little debt. Cox & Kings instead carried heavy and rising debt and large receivables and advances, with CFO persistently weak relative to profit. A lender-appointed PwC audit later found ~Rs 4,367 cr siphoned and books manipulated from Apr 2014 to Jun 2019; foreign subsidiaries allegedly forged audit reports and bank statements that Indian auditors consolidated. CP default 26 Jun 2019; stock to ~Rs 2-3 from Rs 250-400. TEST: write down the working-capital sign the business model implies (DMart, Bharti, airlines, travel = negative) and compare with the balance sheet; a mismatch means either a bad business or wrong accounts. Check which audit firm signs each material subsidiary. LESSON: the simplest forensic test is coherence between business model and balance sheet; brand age is not evidence.

data.good_number: a 250-year-old global travel brand, reported profits, international subsidiaries (Holidaybreak UK)
data.test_that_catches_it: does working-capital sign match the business model; CFO vs PAT; who audits subsidiaries; pledge and CP dependence
data.why_misleading: a business that collects cash in advance showed high receivables, loans/advances and rising debt; foreign subsidiaries' books were forged

title: Hidden trap: Cox & Kings' 250-year brand and reported profits
